\section*{01 - The Challenge}
\section*{The number on the slide is not the number at the bedside}
The central question\par
Focal cortical dysplasia
  a subtle malformation of the cortex that causes epilepsy and is easy to miss on MRI.
  These lesions can be small and low-contrast, so a detector that works on obvious cases can still fail on the subtle ones that bring a patient to imaging in the first place.\par
Oracle localization
  a result reported under the assumption that the correct region is already known.
  When a method is told which lobe to search, its recovery numbers are an upper bound on what a real pipeline could achieve, because a real pipeline has to find the region first.\par

\section*{Three threads, one standard of evidence}
\subsection*{Detecting Subtle Epileptic Lesions}
\textit{Structural-Functional Integration for Enhanced Detection of Subtle Epileptogenic Lesions}\par
What the pipeline uses
    annotated localization zones, not a raw EEG signal.
    The zones come from clinical annotations and anatomical parcels, so the pipeline is told where to look. It does not read an EEG trace, which is why every recovery number here is an upper bound rather than an achievable EEG-guided result.\par
14 of 24\par
missed lesions recovered (58\%) under oracle localization, against 1.4 expected by chance, P \&lt; 0.001\par

\textbf{Limitations.} The pipeline relies on manual clinical annotations for the localization zones. The sensitivity against false-positive tradeoff is not fully characterized. Some hyperparameters, including the 0.90 outside-zone threshold, were chosen without full justification. And the method can harm well-detected cases, which is reported rather than hidden. What is next is an end-to-end pipeline that extracts localization directly from raw EEG, so the oracle assumption is removed.\par
